chunks.text: All right. Good afternoon, everyone. It's Ms. Hall, is it? No, Karen Adair from MPI. Oh, sorry, no. We've got SAFE on via Zoom. Oh, SAFE. But that's all right. No, feel free. You're from MPI. Feel free to remain there. That's all right. We've got our submitter coming in by...
And you're next, so you might as well stay there. Thank you. Keep the seats warm. And we've got our submitter ready to go.

Kia ora. Just wondering if you've got me there. Oh, yes. Good afternoon, Ms. Hall. I'm Greg O'Connor, I'm the chair of the Petitions Committee. Just introducing ourselves for your sake and for the submitters who are in the room already. My right- Greg Fleming, National MP for Maungakiekie. Andrew Bayly from Whangarei.

Green MP Brown, Green List MP, very shortly going to be replaced by Steve Abel, who'll be missing as well. And I'm an ex-SAFE member, so welcome. Oh. Good start. All right. We're not declaring that as a conflict. Right. Now, welcome. We've got you for 10 minutes.

Take your submission as read, but speak to it and hopefully leave some time for questions. And just so you know- Just checking you can hear me okay... all the following submitters from MPI and SPCA are in the room here now. Great, thank you. Just checking you can hear me okay in terms of audio.

I can hear you very well, and if I can, probably the others can too. Wonderful. All right. Kia ora koutou. Ko Emily Hall toku ingoa. I'm a campaign manager at SAFE, and on behalf of the Commissioner for Animals Alliance, thank you for the opportunity to speak with you today. I'll get right into it. This petition calls on Parliament to create an independent commissioner for animals to provide impartial oversight and accountability of our animal welfare system.

At its core, this is about a simple principle, that laws and systems intended to protect vulnerable groups should have non-partisan oversight. This principle is recognized in many other areas. For example, we have independent commissioners and officers of Parliament to help protect the interests of children, the environment, human rights, our aged community, and privacy.

However, animals, despite being recognized as sentient beings and protected under law, do not have impartial non-partisan representation. Let's look at the problem we're trying to solve. The Animal Welfare Act is generally regarded as a strong piece of legislation, and the issue here isn't that we lack animal welfare laws.

The issue is that without non-biased, independent oversight, our animal welfare system is failing the animals it was designed to protect. The Animal Welfare Act itself is now 25 years old, and many of the other laws and frameworks that affect animals are older still. Much of our animal welfare regulatory system is no longer fit for purpose, and independent oversight of that system is urgently needed to improve transparency, accountability, and effectiveness.

Currently, responsibility for animal welfare sits within structures that also hold responsibility for growing agricultural productivity, increasing exports, and supporting industry that profit from the use of animals. This results in real or perceived conflicts of interest and leads to animal welfare considerations frequently falling secondary to industry and economic objectives.

This doesn't mean the people working within the system are failing. Rather, it means the system itself lacks an independent mechanism capable of ensuring animal welfare outcomes are genuinely prioritized. So why is an independent commissioner needed? The remit of a commissioner would not replace existing agencies or advisory committees.

Rather, it would address what is currently missing, and that is independent scrutiny. MPI has, through its own admission to this committee, identified that concerns about the agency's dual responsibility have existed for many years. A report released by the New Zealand Animal Law Association in December last year highlighted the pressing need for independent oversight of animal welfare and identified several issues with the current system, including conflicts of interest, lack of independent oversight, poor enforcement of legislation, and insufficient

resourcing. The findings of NZALA's report present a clear case for establishing an independent commissioner to provide oversight of this framework and enforcement of the Animal Welfare Act. SPCA has submitted that this is an opportunity to recommend targeted and proportionate reform that will both strengthen our animal welfare system and help ensure it meets statutory obligations and public expectations.

It's also worth noting the support that is emerging across the political spectrum. The Green Party has long supported the establishment of an independent commissioner. National MP Barbara Kuriger has attended our last few parliamentary events and been supportive of the concept, and discussions with Labor indicate that their main concern appears to be cost rather than the concept itself.

I'd now like to turn to the importance of public confidence. When decision-making processes are perceived as being influenced by industries, organizations, or individuals with direct economic interest in the outcome, public trust can be significantly undermined. New Zealanders have high expectations of how animals are treated, and polling undertaken last year by SAFE and Verian confirmed that people certainly expect more than what the current system is delivering.
This polling told us that 96% of Kiwis believe it's important to protect animals from cruelty and neglect. In addition to that

Decisions relating to animal welfare law are made by an independent and impartial party, and 67% support the idea of New Zealand having a commissioner to oversee animal welfare. An independent commissioner would certainly help strengthen public confidence that decisions are being made transparently and with the welfare of animals as a priority, rather than being shaped by industry objectives or vested interests.

To briefly address the topic of budget, I recognize that any proposal for a new public office needs to be considered alongside competing funding priorities and the responsible use of public resources. Through the identification of synergies and systemic improvements, a commissioner for animals will improve overall efficiencies in New Zealand's approach to the oversight of animal welfare and enforcement of our legislation now and into the future.

Establishing a commissioner to improve our nation's approach to animal welfare will not only uphold the value we place on the health and well-being of animals, but it will also help protect our international and trade reputations. We do not believe this to be a question of can New Zealand afford to do this? Rather, that we can't afford not to.

I'll speak briefly now about what I'd like to think of as constructive reform. Unfortunately, this is not a radical proposal. It is proportionate and supported not only by the SPCA and NZALA, but also by the Commissioner for Animals Alliance, a strong and diverse coalition of 22 animal protection organizations united behind this call for reform.

This follows a model already familiar within our constitutional framework, with Parliament recognizing issues that are important enough to warrant an independent oversight body. A few examples being the Commissioner for the Environment, who provides independent scrutiny of environmental issues, the Children's Commissioner, who provides independent oversight of matters relating to children, and the Privacy Commissioner, who provides independent oversight, monitoring, and reporting on matters affecting privacy.

This proposal applies the same governance principle, that our animal welfare system depends on the strength and integrity of the framework supporting it. Ultimately, this is about ensuring the system functions as intended and that the welfare of animals is genuinely prioritized.

Finally, I'd like to outline why we believe a Commissioner for Animals would benefit New Zealand and why Parliament should support this petition. The request in this petition is measured and reasonable. We're not asking Parliament to resolve every animal issue right now. We're asking Parliament to acknowledge that a system responsible for protecting hundreds of millions of sentient beings should have independent oversight and accountability.

And the establishment of a Commissioner for Animals would help ensure better transparency and accountability, adequate consideration of scientific evidence, it would bolster public confidence, and it would ensure a more consistent application of animal welfare legislation. These are all goals that are not only in the best interests of animals, they're also in the best interest of regulators, policymakers, industry, and the public. We need independent oversight and accountability to support a system we can all rely on and be proud of.

In closing, our animal welfare system is fundamentally broken, and this allows for animals to be the victims of severe cruelty, exploitation, and neglect. The 22 member organizations of the Commissioner for Animals Alliance emphasize the urgent need for improvement to ensure all practices and policies for the care and welfare of animals is developed without bias and are consistent with the intentions of our animal welfare legislation. This is a unique opportunity that would bring New Zealand into line with other countries making significant progress

in strengthening animal welfare protections and oversight. A Commissioner for Animals offers a practical, balanced, and constructive step forward, supporting the government's commitment to animal welfare and resulting in significantly improved outcomes for animals. I respectfully request the Petitions Committee recommends that the House considers establishing a Commission for Animals as an important step in improving New Zealand's animal welfare system.

Thank you for your time, and I welcome any questions. All right. Thank you very much. We've got time for probably a couple of questions. Mr. Abel. Yeah. Thank you so much for the excellent submission. The obvious question is going to be where best to spend budget to benefit animals, and you usefully laid out the various expenditures for NAWAC and so forth and the government allocation to welfare enforcement.

And is it your view that spending money on a commissioner is more useful than, for example, increasing the capability of MPI or having an independent animal welfare agency that is better resourced to enforce the current Animal Welfare Act? That's a great question. Thank you, Steve.

The future vision really would be a Ministry for Animals, but a commissioner feels like a practical and reasonable and constructive step that will address the myriad issues inherent within our animal welfare system and deliver immediate positive outcomes. But in terms of the budget, I'm not quite sure I interpreted the question correctly. But essentially, what am I trying to say? The CFA would sit alongside existing enforcement agencies and advisory committees and strengthen those existing frameworks by providing oversight and accountability rather than replacing their

roles. So we see the key differences being that commissioner would look at the system as a whole, rather than carrying out one part of it. So n- Which none of these existing agencies or advisory committees currently do. So the commissioner would provide that accountability and transparency, and most importantly, this would address what is missing, and that's that independent oversight of a system where conflicts of interest and interest recapture are, quite frankly, rife.

I realize that doesn't exactly answer your question about diverting funding, and I don't think I'm capable to answer parliamentary budget questions, but does that- No, I think that's a very useful response because you're essentially saying the oversight and vision for how to best address animal welfare issues is lacking in the current system, and a commissioner would bring that.

Well, that- That's right. Yeah. Just one question. Would you anticipate, contemplate that this role would take any operational functions off any existing agencies or it would be, as you said, oversight only? Again, I don't feel like I'm qualified to get into the nitty-gritty about how the role of a commissioner would be divvied up within Parliament.

But again, just to reiterate, that this would address what is missing, and that is that vital independent oversight of a system where conflicts arise. It'll provide a central point of coordination and oversight across the wider animal welfare system, which is currently fragmented across multiple agencies and sectors. And again, we see this as comparable to other parliamentary bodies, oversight bodies such as the Privacy Commissioner for Children and Young People, Children's Commission, where there are ministries as well and other agencies undertaking specific roles, but

the commissioner sits as a independent oversight body alongside them. All right. Look, thank you very much. Our time is now up. So look, thank you, and you're welcome to remain on while we hear from the other agencies now. Thank you. I will. Thank you very much. Thank you. Thank you. All right, now welcome to MPI.

So, the floor is yours. 10 minutes. Take your submission as read, but put some in, it'd be appreciated. Thank you, Mr. Chair, and thank you for the opportunity to speak to MPI's evidence that was presented to you. New Zealand has a strong and internationally respected animal welfare regulatory system.

The Animal Welfare Act provides a robust legislative foundation supported by codes of welfare, regulations, monitoring, enforcement, independent advice, public consultation, and judicial oversight. Strong animal welfare outcomes are very important in their own right and underpin confidence in New Zealand's food and fiber sector and our international reputation.

MPI leads the animal welfare regulatory system through a dedicated and experienced animal health and welfare team. The senior level representation appearing before the committee today reflects the importance MPI places on animal welfare and the strength of leadership supporting the system across MPI's business units.

MPI also has a strong culture of regulatory stewardship and continuous improvement across all of our regulatory systems. The Inspector General Regulatory Systems reports directly to the Director General of MPI and independently reviews all of MPI's regulatory systems and identifies opportunities to strengthen performance and public confidence.

One of the strengths of New Zealand's animal welfare system is that responsibility and oversight are shared across a number of institutions. Parliament sets the legislative framework. Ministers are accountable for decisions. Independent advisory committees provide expert advice. MPI and SPCA undertake compliance and enforcement functions, and the courts provide independent scrutiny.

Public consultation also gives New Zealanders a direct voice in the development of animal welfare standards and regulations. Together, these different roles create multiple checks, balances, and opportunities for independent challenge. Independent advice is a cornerstone of the system. The National Animal Welfare Advisory Committee, NAWAC, and the National Animal Ethics Advisory Committee, NAEC, are statutory advisory committees established under the Animal Welfare Act and provide independent and expert advice to ministers.

Together, they provide an important independent voice within the animal welfare system and bring expertise from science, animal welfare, animal ethics, and commercial animal use. Scientific evidence and expert advice are central to the recommendations provided by both committees.

NAWAC's code development processes include public consultation, ensuring a broad range of perspectives are heard and considered. MPI is confident that compliance and enforcement arrangements are delivering. Between 2023 and 2025, MPI responded to 4,770 reported cases, undertook 1,178 proactive investigations, received 2,967 referrals, and issued just over 1,700 infringements.

MPI filed 39 animal welfare prosecutions in the calendar year ending December 2025. As of June 2026, 79 MPI prosecutions were before the courts We have also increased our focus on proactive and preventative activity to identify issues earlier and support better long-term outcomes for animals.

MPI works closely with the SPCA through a strong co-regulatory partnership and provides $6.6 million annually to support SPCA inspectorate functions. The SPCA therefore plays an important dual role in the system as both a co-regulator and an advocate for animal welfare.

In 2025, the Inspector General Regulatory Systems completed an independent review of New Zealand's animal welfare regulatory system. The review concluded that the system has served New Zealand well, is built on a solid foundation, and is fundamentally sound. The review also identified opportunities for continuous improvement in areas such as governance, stakeholder engagement, performance monitoring, and code review processes.

MPI has accepted the review's recommendations. We have an implementation program of work underway and is using the recommendations to further strengthen an already sound and effective system. Overall, MPI is confident that New Zealand has a strong animal welfare regulatory system that combines independent advice, robust enforcement, public accountability, and a commitment to continuous improvement. Thank you.

Just a question. Who appointed the Inspector General? Who do they report to? The Inspector General is appointed by the Director General of MPI-... our chief executive. Right. So they were making recommendations back to MPI. That's right. Yep. Steve O. Can I ask a couple questions on this one?

Yeah. The first one is, how readily can the likes of NAWAC and NIAC criticize the efficacy of MPI's strategy- Mm... or implementation of its work? And I think in the context of the ability of the Commissioner for the Environment, for example, to take that very broad overview, not to have to deal with the day-to-day business of scrutinizing pieces of legislation, but to actually paint a broader vision of what could be happening in the environmental space.

And would that not be a useful thing to have in the animal welfare space, given its importance to us as an intrinsic value, but also in terms of our international reputation? NAWAC can provide independent advice to the- Yes... to the minister. So there's two things.

It has its work program that they agree directly with the minister, but they also have the opportunity to pick up areas and issues of concern, and you've seen that happen in the past. I guess it's an issue for ... If you think about the parallel with the environment, you've still got insert and EPA doing all the compliance activity, the legislative activity, the legislative development. So,

NAWAC and NIAC probably provide an equivalent role- Right... but in a slightly different form. That's sort of my point. So- Mm... the argument would be that it would enhance the overall efficacy and integrity of the whole system to have a Commissioner for Animals.

The system as it currently is with NAWAC and NIAC, with both scientific expertise, veterinary expertise people from the NGO, but also people who are involved in farming or working with animals, gives them ability to take a very balanced view and look for opportunities for improvement.

And NAWAC and NIAC don't always agree with MPI on the view. They are genuinely independent bodies which balance their advice based on the act. So- Is it fair to say that the scope of their work has been altered in the last three or four years to focus more on the commercial or sort of farming aspect?

And how was that instruction delivered? Was that delivered through the MPI or directly from the minister? So ministers of the day make a call on where they want NAWAC and NIAC to focus. Directly to them or through MPI? They go directly to- Directly to the- And the chairs meet directly with the minister to discuss their work program. To discuss the work program and the prioritization- Mm ... of the work program.

So doesn't that leave MPI out of it altogether then in that regard? It's a little bit hard. If that's the case, it's a little bit difficult to say that MPI have- So ministers will get advice from- Can rely on them if they're not actually instructing them. Ministers will get advice from multiple sources, obviously.

And in the system, they get advice from From two sources. They get advice directly from NAWAC and NIAC, depending on what the issue is, and they get advice from MPI. So ministers will normally ask us what our view is, but then they will- Where would you get information from if it wasn't through those two organizations, though?

Where would you get sufficient information to be able to advise the minister if it wasn't through those two organizations? Through talking to stakeholders. You meet regularly with SPCA, who provide advice and information to us in terms of the issues they are seeing. So for example, in the last parliamentary term, SPCA have championed the regulations and updating on dog tethering, which the minister agreed to take forward, and there's conversations around other things that the SPCA is ongoing at the moment that SPCA

see as a priority in companion animals. You meet regularly with the industry, with the NGOs, with SAFE, with a range of stakeholders to inform MPI's view. So if the minister narrowed the scope of the work of those two organizations, does the ministry have the ability to backfill, whether it be perhaps the information for work wasn't being done that was previously being done by those two organizations?

You wouldn't have any information then to rely on, would you, if that work was previously being done by those two organizations? NAWAC and NIAC. Yeah. Not sure where you're-- So- It's probably not a fair question in your position, so I'll leave it at that.

Sorry. Was that- Yeah, no, go ahead. I was just going to say, we have a normal kind of process- There's no one from NAWAC here, is there? From a- No, there's not No. No. From a public service kind of perspective, we have a regular process of looking at all the international research ourselves.

And so we do a whole lot of our own kind of research. We have a range of technical experts who work at MPI, and MPI does hold the secretariat for NAWAC as well. So we do have a relationship with NAWAC, and with NIAC as well. Secretariat for both of them. Yeah. Sorry, one last question.

Yeah, my last one would be, therefore, I think is there not some degree of challenge in them being able to give purely independent advice insofar as their secretariat is held in such a way as they have to find outcomes and achieve outcomes in working with the minister and working with MPI, that a commissioner would be unbound by? A commissioner would have an ability to have a greater freedom to be candid and frank in criticizing or

commending the efficacy of what was going on at the MPI level or at any level. And isn't that exactly why a commissioner would be a helpful addition to the system? I'd probably say the opposite, to be perfectly frank, because NAWAC in particular, because I think the focus seems to be more on NAWAC's role than NIAC's role, which is around research, education, testing and teaching.

So NAWAC, it's not just an advisory role. Well, it is an advisory role, but they actually develop the codes. They actually provide recommendations on which elements of the codes need to then be reinforced in regulation. So they have quite an active role in ensuring the regulatory framework around animals is addressing the right issue. They look at the research.

They are supported by your secretariat. But that secretariat is quite careful around keeping the independence of the discussion with NAWAC. And the respective chairs that have had have been very clear about retaining their ability to meet with the minister and provide their free and frank advice to the minister.

And it doesn't always line up with where MPI is coming from, and sometimes it doesn't line up with where the ministers are coming from. So they take their statutory independent role incredibly seriously. All right. Look, thank you very much. Very useful.
And from the SPCA, welcome to the table.

All right. Welcome. Thank you, Patience. Of course. Thank you for having us here today. It's very good to be back. My name's Anya Dale. I'm the Chief Scientific Officer for the SPCA. I've talked to you a number of times as a committee before, and with me is Marie McIninch, who is a Senior Scientific Officer in farmed animals. And we're really pleased to be able to talk to you about this matter today because, of course, the functioning of the animal welfare system is obviously of critical importance to the SPCA.

We have around 70 inspectors in the field, 110 auxiliary officers. We respond to about 15,000 plus complaints per year. We audit animal welfare standards on certified farms. We have about 100 million animals under that program. We provide education to children in schools about animal welfare and responsible animal ownership in every single primary and intermediate school in the country.

And of course, we advocate for changes on behalf of concerned New Zealanders. Just in terms of some history, I have done my two statutory terms on NAWAC. I have done my two statutory terms on NAIAC, so I'm very happy to answer questions at the end if you would like to discuss my perspective.

But as described in our submission, we know that our communities care about animals. A survey we commissioned last month show that 93% of New Zealanders believe it's important to protect farm animals. So clearly it's incredibly important. Our surveys also show that two-thirds of households include a pet, and about nine out of 10 animal owners think of their pets as members of the family, and 85% of New Zealanders strongly agree that the government has a responsibility to ensure high animal welfare standards.

So we will be leaving time for questions, but I'm just going to hand over to Marie to talk about some of the key points from our submission, and then I'm going to talk about a couple of new documents, and then we'll answer questions. Thank you. Thanks, Anya. So I'll just move through it really quickly in terms of a summary of our submission. But our one key point, I suppose is, as we've heard from MPI just now, New Zealand does have institutions that regulate animal welfare and institutions that provide expert independent

advice. But we don't have an independent institution whose job is to look across that whole system, represent animals' interests and the concerns of New Zealanders, and hold the animal welfare system to account. You've heard a lot about the National Animal Welfare Advisory Committee, and I understand that you invited them to make a submission.

But they don't fill that role that a commissioner would fill. There was a question around can they provide feedback on MPI's functioning. NAWAC's functions are listed in Section 57 of the Act. Providing advice on MPI is not one of them. They provide technical advice on animal welfare standards, right?

I'd suggest that this is why you have the petition in front of you today, right? People are feeling this. It may be why you get so many animal petitions and why we know you so well at the end of this term, because you're hearing a lot of feedback about the animal welfare system. We'd put it to you that there is a real leadership gap. Our standards really are falling out of date.

People really are concerned about this out there. Whether you agree that a commissioner is the right solution or not, we really hope that this committee can record those concerns from New Zealanders and from the coalition of organizations that have come to you today. We've put four case studies in our submission around the functioning of the animal welfare system.

I'm not going to go through them all, but I just wanted to highlight one of them, and that was, I think it's quite topical, the need for updated standards for companion animals. And obviously, there's been some work on tethered dogs this term, but we have asked for a lot more than that because we need a lot more than that.

The fact is that the standards our inspectors rely on have been allowed to age while the frontline demands on our inspectors have become more complex. Recent reporting has highlighted threats and abuse directed at SPCA staff. Our inspectors are now issued stab-proof vests. We conservatively estimate that up to 20% of call-to jobs have identifiable co-indicators of family violence, and we are enforcing standards that are a couple of decades old now.

At the same time, we're seeing these new and growing welfare issues. There are no specific animal welfare regulations for businesses like doggy daycares, and it's been reported on recently. No regulations governing commercial dog breeding as the dog population explodes. And rabbits, New Zealand's third most popular companion animal, still don't have any minimum welfare standards at all.

So while the problems have evolved, the regulatory framework has not kept up. In terms of the question around backfilling that work when NAWAC has been instructed to focus on farmed animals, we tried to backfill that work using charitable resources and donations. We drafted three new codes of welfare for dogs, cats, and rabbits and submitted that a few years ago now. We had an agreement with MPI and NAWAC to progress those codes. We invested significant resources in that.

We worked with stakeholders. We were in a consultation, but that work stopped when the minister directed NAWAC to stop working on it. That is within the minister's powers, but that's the point. NAWAC cannot fill the role that the petitioners are asking for. They are subject to political directions of the day. There is no plan to progress minimum standards for these three groups of animals related to companion animals that we're aware of.

This country recently earned a D grade in the World Animal Protection global rankings for regulation for companion animals. We had earned an A grade back in 2020 That's just one of the examples in our submission, and we trust you've read the others, including previous recommendations by the Regulations Select Committee.

And I'll hand over to Anya to cover a couple of new documents. Karen mentioned the MPI Inspector General review on regulatory systems that we were part of. And just to be clear, it doesn't recommend a commissioner for animal welfare, but some of its findings are highly relevant because it does independently identify many of the structural issues that are actually behind this petition. So for example, it describes dispersed responsibilities across the animal welfare system and says bold system leadership is needed to bring more consistent results.

It acknowledges that many of the codes of welfare are out of date, as we're well aware, and results in uncertainty for those that rely on them. It also found that people within MPI and also outside of MPI were unclear about the direction and the desired outcomes in terms of the animal welfare system, and we agree that stronger leadership is needed.

Obviously, MPI have responded to strengthen its internal governance, and that is including refreshing the animal welfare steering committee and establishing a plan to engage with stakeholders, and we really welcome those measures. But we think that there's a difference between internal system leadership and what this petition is actually asking for, which is independent oversight.

So for example, this system review actually didn't interrogate the companion animal industry at all, nor did it consider whether New Zealand's expectations were met when they refer to animal welfare issues. This petition obviously is fronted by a number of animal rescue groups, and we hear from them every single day.

We know they expect more from us, but despite repeated advocacy, we're unable to get the companion animal regulations and codes back into the system, with the exception of the Dog Code of Welfare, which has just been added to NAWAC's work program, which is fantastic. And when you look through the report- Sorry, which one's been added? The- Dogs. But just added, so no work has begun, obviously, other than what SPCA did, which included 400 submissions from key stakeholders that we addressed.

Also, key stakeholders in the animal welfare system aren't referred to or listed in there. For example, animal rescues or wildlife rehabbers or companion animal industries like dog daycares. Even for farmed animals, they do list farm animal industries, but not consumers or supermarkets, and so we suggest that perhaps someone with a bit of distance from MPI may help.

In addition, just the other document that I'd like to refer to is that we've made an OIA request because we were very interested in obviously what is happening with NAWAC and NIAT. Well, particularly NAWAC because that seems to be the committee that the government has focused on, and particularly in relation to the coalition agreements between National and New Zealand First and National and ACT.

It wasn't released, but the ombudsman did intervene on our behalf. And just in terms of the briefings from MPI to NAWAC, they do state that in the official's view, they think NAWAC has strayed beyond its statutory role in doing things like publishing opinions that the public can read, which are actually very useful.

Other things is that NAWAC's functioning to meet its statutory obligation. A review could have educational value for both NAWAC and MPI, and a review could be used to lead culture change. And also, the package obviously included suggestions to fix NAWAC, including clarifying NAWAC's role, changing membership criteria to better reflect the sector and industry knowledge, and rebalancing practical and economic considerations. Now, that's really important because under the act, it says they may consider them. Obviously, the letter of expectation from the

minister says to give high priority to them. That was received. So NAWAC is a useful advisory committee, but they are subject to a number of constraints. So then they can't be an independent watchdog to speak publicly as well as meet their statutory functions.

So to conclude, we do support the aim of the petition, and regardless of the committee's ultimate recommendation, we do ask the committee to record the concerns of multiple stakeholders who brought this petition forward to you, and we're very happy to take questions. Sure. Yeah. Thank you. Mr. Chair. You've, in a sense, pre-responded to the points that MPI were making before.

You said that the existing institutional arrangements are limited in scope and effectiveness, and while bodies such as the National Animal Welfare Advisory Committee and the National Animal Ethics Advisory Committee provide technical advice, they have very limited mandates compared to that of a commissioner. And you go on to say that NAWAC's reliance on the eye for resourcing and secretariat support, combined with its exposure to changing ministerial direction, limits its independence, visibility, and ability to prioritize animal welfare. That's quite a statement to

make, that even NAWAC is limited in its ability to prioritize animal welfare. Yeah. So my understanding, having had a long relationship with NAWAC, is Minister Hoggard's directive or letter of expectation is the first time that a minister has actually intervened with NAWAC's work program.

Yeah. And that was to pause all companion animal work and work on the production codes, which obviously are critically important, and we agree with them. We've provided alternate suggestions about how both can be progressed because both are important. Yeah. We've got time for a brief one, Mr. Bailey.

Thank you. Well, first of all, thank you for Fronting up and saying what you've just said, so that's good. You talked about leadership and one option, obviously, is commission, but there are other options, obviously. You talked about the intervention of the minister.

Mm-hmm. And then you've talked about these code deficiencies. Mm. So I'm just setting aside what the petition is talking about. Structurally, what would you do to get that overarching, and where do you think that responsibility lies? The second part of it, these codes, and we assured a lot of deficiencies in the code across even farm animals as well as companion animals.

Is that a resourcing issue, leadership issue, or why have we gone from number one to where we are now in the companion animals, for instance? Sorry. There you go. No, that's good. There's a lot of questions in one there. Okay. So I'll do my best to go about it. And look, I do have to say we're limited for time.

Okay. We've got other submitters coming, so we do have to respect the- Yeah. So I'll be quick. I think that NAWAC is not truly independent because they're intertwined with MPI in every respect and area of policy and area there. But one way that we could address this is for NAWAC to be truly independent, have its own budget, and manage its own staff, which are not within MPI. So that is one possibility that that could happen.

In relation to codes, there certainly is efficiencies that can be done by getting stakeholder groups to do a huge amount of work. It is problematic when that work's not progressed. We invested years of work into that. I do know that having been on NAWAC and been on NAIAC, you are limited in terms of what you can progress, and that does lead to the fact that what you talked about, which is a resourcing issue.

You could make them much more functioning committees if they met more often and had independent resourcing that they could utilize. At the moment, NAWAC meets three times a year. Obviously, they have some subcommittees that meet between that time, and work has progressed on various codes. But it is-- If you meet three times a year, it's difficult to progress a huge amount.

So it could be addressed. Okay. Just finally, bearing in mind with what going back to the petition, which is establishment of a commissioner. And even the advocate of it doesn't see that it would take any operation functions off any existing agencies.
